newsitem.title: USA: Less influential role seen for Gingrich next year.
newsitem.headline: Less influential role seen for Gingrich next year.

text.p: Speaker Newt Gingrich faces a diminished role next year no matter which party wins control of the House of Representatives -- a sea change from his fiery championing of the Republican revolution two years ago.

Nationwide, the controversial Georgian was blamed for two government shutdowns last winter and became the lightning rod for Democratic attacks on his party. Many Republicans are taking pains to distance themselves from him, and he is under ethics investigations into whether he wrongly used a tax-exempt foundation for political purposes.

If the party retains control of the House, re-elected Republicans will not owe him the allegiance they felt in 1994 when he was credited with engineering the party's return to power after 40 years in the minority. A re-elected Speaker Gingrich, who once vowed not to compromise, would be forced to abandon his aggressive stance in order to pass his agenda.
If Democrats regain the majority, Gingrich has said he will decline the post of Minority Leader and will become simply Representative Newt Gingrich of the 6th district of Georgia.

"The job of the Republican leadership in a minority would be reduced to simply opposing (Democrats), to be negative," said Gingrich, who dismissed as "ridiculous" reports that he would resign rather than face an ethics investigation spearheaded by Democrats.

His public approval rating fell to a low of 19 percent in June but recovered when Congress adjourned after averting a fresh budget crisis. A New York Times/CBS poll of registered voters this week showed him with a 31 percent approval rating.

"He made such a public name for himself at the beginning of the 104th (Congress) that it became the reverse of Teflon, criticisms stuck to him," political scientist Ron Shaiko of American University said.

Analyst Norman Ornstein of the conservative American Enterprise Institute said a Republican victory would still not be a mandate for Gingrich as 1994 was held to be. The 104th Congress ended with 235 Republicans, 198 Democrats and 1 independent who usually votes with the Democrats.
Ornstein noted, "It is going to be a tougher situation. He will not start out (as in 1995) with the party not just behind him but in awe of his leadership."
In 1995, there were 73 freshmen Republicans who owed their election to the firebrand Gingrich and many House veterans thrilled to be in charge of committees at last.

Ornstein predicted Gingrich and Republicans would find it difficult to be on the offensive against President Bill Clinton, who appeared to be headed for a solid victory over Republican presidential candidate Bob Dole.
"It's going to be compromise or nothing," he said.

While the outcome in the House is considered a toss-up, Gingrich predicted this week he will pick up from 6 to 20 Republican seats on Nov. 5. If so, it would be the first time since 1928 that Republicans held onto a House majority for a second term. Republicans had a majority only in 1947-49 and 1953-55.
Re-election from his suburban Atlanta district seems assured with a reported 14 percent lead over cookie magnate Michael Coles, a Democrat.

Rumours that Gingrich will face a challenge as Speaker of the House are denied by congressional Republican aides. Analysts note that party loyalties are divided among the other three top House Republicans, making a palace coup dangerous and unlikely. The one who lost a challenge to Gingrich would be permanently outside the speaker's inner circle.
As Shaiko noted, even one of the most liberal Republicans, Connie Morella of Maryland, supports Gingrich for Speaker.

George Washington University's Christopher Arterton predicted Republicans will hold onto the House and Gingrich will be re-elected speaker. "There are many Newt Gingrich's and we will see a different Newt Gingrich than we did in 1995," he added.

Aterton said there will be a half-year chance for major legislative compromises between Gingrich, chastened by his experience as speaker, and Democrats and Clinton, who were forced in the past two years to move to the centre.
"One might see an era of goodwill returning to Washington, a striking development" after recent acrimony, he said.
